\chapter{Talking About Ideas --- Hedging From Doubt, and From Inference}
\label{ch:ideas}
\hlchaptermodality{271}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put an idea forward in Spanish while marking how sure I am of it, and tell an admission of ignorance from a claimed inference.}

Complete ES-C271-supongo-que: state one idea three ways -- bare, hedged with quizas, and hedged with supongo que -- and say what each does to your commitment.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[quizás]{quizás — saying it without claiming it}

\label{lesson:ES-C271-quizas}



\begin{quote}
An argument needs one more thing: a way to put an idea forward while admitting you might be wrong.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item aunque — the concession that closed the last chapter.
  \item en mi opinión — marking a claim as yours.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ki-ZÁS}, stress on the last syllable, and the accent says so. You will also see \textbf{quizá}, without the \emph{-s}; both are standard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{quizás} — \textquotedblleft{}maybe, perhaps.\textquotedblright{}

It is a fossilised question. Latin \textbf{qui sapit} — \emph{\textquotedblleft{}who knows?\textquotedblright{}} — said often enough that it stopped being a question and became a word meaning \emph{perhaps}. The \emph{sapit} is the same root as \textbf{savoir}, \textbf{sapient} and, at some distance, \textbf{sage}: knowing.

English did the identical thing twice over. \emph{Perhaps} is \emph{per} + \emph{hap}, \textquotedblleft{}by chance\textquotedblright{}; \emph{maybe} is \emph{may be}. Every language seems to build its hedges by wearing down a phrase that once admitted ignorance out loud.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is a \textbf{hedge}: it lowers your commitment without lowering your meaning. \emph{Es difícil} claims. \emph{Quizás es difícil} offers.

Set beside what you already have, you now hold three settings on the same dial — \emph{en mi opinión} marks a claim as yours, \emph{quizás} marks it as uncertain, and a bare statement claims outright.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{quizás} — stress the end
  \item a claim, then the same claim hedged
  \item what Latin \emph{qui sapit} asked (\emph{who knows?})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What question is hidden inside \emph{quizás}? (\emph{Qui sapit} — \textquotedblleft{}who knows?\textquotedblright{}) What does a hedge lower — your meaning, or your commitment? (Your commitment.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[supongo que]{supongo que — the hedge that shows its reasoning}

\label{lesson:ES-C271-supongo-que}



\begin{quote}
The second hedge, and it is not the same as the first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item quizás — the hedge that admits uncertainty.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{su-PON-go ke}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{supongo que} — \textquotedblleft{}I suppose that.\textquotedblright{}

Take it apart and it is beautifully literal: Latin \textbf{sub-} (\textquotedblleft{}under\textquotedblright{}) plus \textbf{ponere} (\textquotedblleft{}to place\textquotedblright{}). To suppose is to \textbf{place something underneath} — to slide an assumption under an argument so the argument can stand on it.

That \emph{ponere} is everywhere in English once you see it: \textbf{compose} (place together), \textbf{impose} (place upon), \textbf{depose}, \textbf{postpone}, \textbf{position}. And \emph{supongo} is exactly English \textbf{suppose}, arrived by the same road.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\emph{Quizás} and \emph{supongo que} hedge differently, and the difference is worth keeping.

\emph{Quizás} says: I do not know. \emph{Supongo que} says: I have not been told, but it follows.

The first admits ignorance; the second claims an inference. In an argument they do opposite work — one steps back from a claim, the other quietly offers a reason for it.

With this the chapter's four moves are complete: name an abstract thing, name a whole idea, hedge from uncertainty, and hedge from inference.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{supongo que} …, finishing it however you like
  \item the same idea with \emph{quizás} instead, and hear what changed
  \item three English words built on \emph{ponere}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sub-} + \emph{ponere} mean literally? (To place underneath.) Which hedge admits ignorance, and which claims an inference? (\emph{Quizás}; \emph{supongo que}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Three settings on one dial}

\label{lesson:ES-C271-practice}



\begin{quote}
Two hedges, and a bare statement between them. This is where you feel the difference rather than read it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Take one idea of your own — anything you could argue about — and say it three times.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the bare claim. No hedge. Hear how much you have committed to.
  \item the same claim with \emph{quizás} in front. You have not changed the idea; you have changed how far you will defend it.
  \item the same claim again with \emph{supongo que}. Now you are not admitting ignorance — you are offering an inference, and inviting the listener to check your reasoning rather than your confidence.
\end{itemize}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which of the three you would use with a stranger, and why
  \item which one an argument is hardest to answer with, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which hedge admits you do not know? (\emph{Quizás}.) Which one claims a reason you have not been given? (\emph{Supongo que}.) What did the Latin behind each one mean — \textquotedblleft{}who knows?\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}to place underneath\textquotedblright{}?
\end{tcolorbox}
